proposals.name: Mechanistic hypothesis that is itself put at risk
proposals.instruction: Score how far the abstract goes beyond reporting that something works to naming a mechanism and then testing the mechanism itself. 10: the text states an explicit causal hypothesis about why an effect occurs, derives from it at least one intervention or prediction whose result would discriminate the hypothesis (not merely improve a number), and reports running it. 5: a mechanism is named and a fix is built on it, but nothing in the reported evidence could have contradicted the mechanism -- only the fix is tested. 2: a mechanism is asserted post hoc to rationalise an observed gain. 0: purely procedural -- a technique is applied and outcomes reported with no account of why it should work.
proposals.rationale: R01 states the two-domain hypothesis and then does three things that put it at risk (dropping clean images, splitting BN statistics, forcing train/test BN consistency); R13 defines supervision complexity and uses it to predict when early stopping, temperature scaling and staged online distillation should help. R04 similarly measures the network state to test whether early-phase changes are label-agnostic. Contrast R26 and R08, which name plausible causes (foreground/background imbalance, missing relations, facet granularity) but only ever test the patch, never the diagnosis -- a scorecard asking 'is a mechanism given?' cannot separate these, while a reader who asks 'was the mechanism at risk?' can.

proposals.name: Deflationary finding about standard practice or own machinery
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract commits to a result that could disappoint someone, including the authors. 10: a central reported finding undercuts a widely used component, a standard assumption, or the authors' own preferred apparatus, and it is stated specifically enough to be checked (for example: a standard normalization layer is harmful in this regime; most modern components of the studied family turn out to be unnecessary; the framework's own robustness assumption fails). 5: a limitation is acknowledged but is peripheral to the claims. 0: every statement in the abstract is a gain, an improvement, or a capability; nothing reported would trouble any reader.
proposals.rationale: R18 concludes that only a very few modern diffusion components matter and that a classical denoising autoencoder largely suffices -- a result against the grain of the machinery being studied. R04 reports that deep networks are NOT robust to sign-preserving reinitialisation, a negative about the very framework it borrows. R05 argues the standard concentration-of-measure programme fails to characterise intrinsic robustness, and R40 argues a universally used layer can simply be frozen. A criterion bank built from 'does the paper demonstrate improvement' will systematically undervalue exactly these, since their content is subtractive.

proposals.name: Contribution is removal or freezing rather than added machinery
proposals.instruction: Score parsimony of the proposal as described. 10: the central contribution removes, freezes, precomputes away, or collapses something (a trained layer, a training stage, a component family, a learned module), and the abstract states plainly what is given up in exchange. 5: a method of ordinary complexity, neither notably simplifying nor notably stacked. 0: the contribution is a stack of several newly named sub-modules, each introduced with its own name and each required for the result, with no account of which are load-bearing.
proposals.rationale: R40 fixes the classifier layer entirely, R18 deconstructs down to a classical autoencoder, R59 removes training from the message-passing module, and R41 replaces heuristic use of a learned model with an explicitly solved optimisation. All sit on the dense_high_card_low side. On the other side R08 stacks prototype learning, a binding mechanism and a dedicated bi-directional binding block, and R23 layers a generation pipeline over a KL objective; explicit-criterion banks tend to reward each named component as evidence of technical contribution, so complexity accrues credit while simplification loses it.

proposals.name: Recasts the problem in a formal frame that buys leverage
proposals.instruction: Score whether a known problem is restated inside a different, precisely named formal frame, and whether the reframing purchases something concrete. 10: the abstract names the reformulation (an optimisation problem, transport between distributions, an extension of a classical theorem, an information-theoretic quantity) AND names what it yields -- a derivation, an explicit formula, a near-optimality statement, a bound, a new estimator. 5: a reformulation is announced but nothing specific follows from it. 0: the problem is stated in its standard form and attacked with the standard toolkit for that form.
proposals.rationale: R41 turns ad hoc use of a learned model into an explicit optimisation and derives near-optimal algorithms from it; R55 reframes docking as transport between distributions and gets unbalanced flow matching; R52 extends Gauss-Markov by permitting bounded bias and derives closed-form estimators; R31 imports rate-distortion estimation to general sources and derives two-sided bounds. This reframing move produces no new benchmark and no new dataset, so it is invisible to criteria keyed on artifacts or wins.

proposals.name: Object of study is a general quantity, not the authors' system
proposals.instruction: Score what the abstract's claims are about. 10: the object studied exists independently of anything the authors built -- the generalization error as a function of scale, the cost of overfitting, the rate-distortion function of a source, the dynamics of the first few hundred training iterations -- and the reported results are stated as properties of that object. 5: a method paper that nonetheless establishes one transferable property of the setting. 0: every claim is a property of the authors' artifact evaluated on chosen datasets; nothing stated would remain true if the artifact were discarded.
proposals.rationale: R09 (functional form of generalization error across model and data scales), R39 (cost of overfitting as a ratio defined for any target), R31 (a fundamental information-theoretic limit) and R04 (the early phase of training as a phenomenon) all make claims that outlive their code. Compare R47 and R57, whose entire content is a property of one compression scheme or one matching pipeline. A scorecard scoring rigour, clarity and evidence item by item cannot register this difference in what the claims are about.

proposals.name: Positions against specific named prior results
proposals.instruction: Score the precision of prior-work positioning inside the abstract. 10: particular prior works are named and the abstract states exactly which part of them is extended, tightened, corrected or contradicted, so a reader can locate the delta without opening the paper. 5: prior work is characterised by approach family with enough specificity to locate it, but no particular result is engaged. 0: prior work appears only in the aggregate as existing methods, previous works, or current approaches, with the delta asserted rather than located.
proposals.rationale: R04 names the exact three findings it is extending, R29 names the specific EF21 analysis whose quadratic-mean dependence it improves to arithmetic mean, R39 names the benign/tempered/catastrophic taxonomy it refines, and R31 names the distributional-assumption and discrete-only predecessors it escapes. Contrast R42, R43, R25 and R23, which engage the literature only as existing methods. Precise positioning is what a domain reader uses to size a contribution, but a criterion bank scoring 'is related work discussed' scores both cases alike.

proposals.name: Stated theory carries the claim rather than restating the construction
proposals.instruction: Judge only the theoretical statements the abstract actually makes. 10: the theoretical result is nontrivial and directly underwrites the headline practical claim -- a guarantee with named dependence, a separation, an equivalence that explains an observed empirical phenomenon. 5: a correct result that supports a side point rather than the main claim. 2: the theorem restates the construction or asserts something close to true by definition, while the language implies it validates the method. 0: 'we theoretically show' with content that is vacuous, circular, or unconnected to what is empirically claimed.
proposals.rationale: R03 offers that incompatible policies are not similar -- close to definitional, yet it is the stated bridge from the objective to the diversity claim; R45 states that its method holds neural collapse optimality when the prototypes were fixed to that geometry by construction. Against these, R13 derives an interplay of teacher accuracy, student margin and supervision complexity that explains existing tricks, R32 proves a margin between in-distribution and OOD scores that its detector actually exploits, and R29 improves a stated complexity dependence. A bank that credits 'includes theoretical analysis' cannot distinguish a load-bearing theorem from a decorative one.

proposals.name: Enumerated items are findings, not deliverables
proposals.instruction: If the abstract uses an enumeration (first/second/third, numbered contributions, bullets), score what is enumerated. 10: the enumerated items are findings about the world or about a phenomenon -- things that were discovered and could have come out otherwise. 5: a mix of findings and produced artifacts. 0: the enumeration lists things the authors made (a dataset, a method, a pipeline, an evaluation suite) as contributions, with the actual results compressed into a closing sentence such as 'extensive experiments validate the effectiveness'. Score 5 by default if no enumeration is used.
proposals.rationale: R01 enumerates two intriguing properties -- both empirical discoveries; R04 enumerates measured facts about early training. Compare R25, whose three major technical contributions are a dataset, an identification method and an induction method, and R43 and R23, which enumerate pipeline stages. Deliverable enumeration is exactly the shape an explicit criterion bank rewards (it makes contributions countable and checkable), while a reader weighs what was learned, not what was shipped.

proposals.name: Something survives when all benchmark numbers are deleted
proposals.instruction: Mentally strike every leaderboard number, percentage and speedup from the abstract and score what remains. 10: a substantive claim remains standing -- a mechanism, a limit, a phenomenon, a design principle -- that a reader could carry into other work; the numbers were evidence for it rather than the content of it. 5: a modest transferable claim remains alongside numbers that do most of the work. 0: what remains is only 'we propose X and it performs better than baselines'; the numbers were the claim.
proposals.rationale: Strip the numbers from R26 (+4.1 AP), R47 (40 percent smaller at 0.5 percent drop), R48 (76 minutes) and R38 (92.7 versus 28.5 ASR) and the residue is largely 'our variant wins'. Strip them from R01 and the two-domain hypothesis and the depth demand survive; from R18 the claim that most modern components are inessential survives; from R05 the argument about label uncertainty survives. A scorecard with items for empirical strength and margin size will grade quantified deltas generously, which is the clearest over-crediting direction in this slice.

proposals.name: Flat declarative register without promotional or interrogative drama
proposals.instruction: Score the register in which claims are made. 10: claims are stated flatly and their scope is visible in the sentence; intensifiers are absent or rare; no rhetorical question is posed in the title or opening that the abstract then answers in the obvious direction. 5: occasional promotional adjectives that do not change what is claimed. 0: the framing rests on hype words (striking, remarkable, comprehensive, novel, significantly) or on a confrontational question, with intensifiers carrying weight the described evidence does not.
proposals.rationale: R15 builds on a free-lunch question and calls its decline striking; R37 stacks comprehensive and novel around an artifact whose stated finding is only 'revealing some limitations'; R43 pairs remarkable with paving the way; R23 leans on significantly outperforms. Against these, R39, R52, R41, R05 and the two-sentence R20 make bare declarative claims. Explicit criterion banks reward the surface markers of ambition and clarity that promotional register supplies, whereas an experienced reader discounts them.

proposals.name: Evidence spans scales or regimes rather than one operating point
proposals.instruction: Score the deliberateness of the evidence sweep described. 10: measurements are taken across a range chosen so that the claim is about a trend or a dependence -- model sizes, dataset sizes, depths, budgets, or several distinct modalities -- and the abstract says the trend holds (or breaks) across that range. 5: two or three settings reported without a range being the point. 0: a single model at a single scale on a single dataset, with the claim implicitly generalised.
proposals.rationale: R09 fits and predicts across model and data scales in both vision and language; R01 pushes depth to an unprecedented point precisely to show the demand is monotone, not incidental; R30 carries its claim from synthetic tasks up to 2.7B parameters; R13 checks across architectures and benchmarks. Sweeps are expensive and are the strongest cheap signal of a claim's robustness, but per-criterion scoring of 'are experiments adequate' typically saturates once several datasets appear, whatever their arrangement.

proposals.name: Builds a controlled probe to isolate a specific capability
proposals.instruction: Score whether the work constructs an instrument whose purpose is isolation rather than scoring. 10: a synthetic task, probe, or deliberately structured ablation is built to isolate one capability or factor, the abstract reports what it revealed, and that reading then drives a design decision or a claim. 5: standard ablations reported after the fact. 0: end-task evaluation only; nothing in the setup could localise where an effect comes from.
proposals.rationale: R30 uses synthetic languages to localise the gap to recall and cross-sequence comparison, then designs a layer for exactly those two abilities; R07 uses linear probing to establish that interpretable directions exist and only then builds control vectors on those directions; R04 instruments the network state directly. Instrument design of this kind is a hallmark of experimental competence, yet it produces no headline number and so is easy for an explicit bank to miss.

proposals.name: Abstract shows the investigative path, including corrections
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the reasoning path is visible. 10: the reader can reconstruct how the result was reached -- the initial idea, why it was inadequate, the correction that followed -- or the work is explicitly framed as a study, a deconstruction, or a diagnosis with a stated philosophy governing it. 5: motivation is given, but the work is presented as arriving fully formed. 0: only the finished artifact and its scores are described; no trace of how or why this design was reached.
proposals.rationale: R29 narrates the route explicitly: an equivalent reformulation requiring impractical machine cloning, then a weighted variant that avoids it, then a circle back to a better analysis of the original method. R18 states its deconstructive philosophy up front and lets the result be wherever the deconstruction lands. R04 reads as a measurement campaign rather than a pitch. This is a strong readable signal of intellectual honesty and control of the problem, and it is precisely the material that a contribution-oriented criterion bank treats as filler.

proposals.name: Diagnosed failure mode generalizes beyond the studied system
proposals.instruction: Locate the failure or gap the paper claims to address and score how far it reaches. 10: the failure is a property of a broad class -- a training regime, an objective, a data condition, a chaining pattern -- recognisable to researchers who never touch the authors' system, and the fix follows from that generality. 5: the failure is specific to a family of methods but the lesson plausibly transfers. 0: the failure is a defect internal to one architecture and the fixes are local patches with no stated implication outside it.
proposals.rationale: R16 identifies three internal defects of one memory architecture and patches each; the diagnosis is careful and legible -- exactly the sort of thing an explicit bank scores well -- but nothing outside that architecture is at stake. Against it, R01 diagnoses a distribution-mixing problem in adversarial training as such, R21 diagnoses why off-policy methods fail whenever the data source is fixed, and R05 diagnoses an omission (labels) in an entire line of analysis. Reach of the diagnosis, not its tidiness, is what a reader trades on.

proposals.name: Names the obstacle that made the combination non-obvious
proposals.instruction: For work that combines existing components, score whether an obstacle is identified and overcome. 10: the abstract names a specific reason the combination is not straightforward (an incompatibility, an instability, a representation that cannot be edited, an approximation that breaks) and states how it was resolved. 5: some difficulty is gestured at without being characterised. 0: the contribution is A plus B, both standard, with each part's strengths listed and the union asserted to inherit them; no obstacle is named, so nothing was apparently hard.
proposals.rationale: R42 presents itself as combining the strengths of two established inference algorithms with the difficulty left unnamed; R47, R45 and R28 read the same way (projective clustering plus embedding factorisation, neural collapse plus incremental learning, several pretrained models fused). Compare R55, which says why existing transport paradigms lack the flexibility needed and generalises flow matching to get it, and R17, which names invalid substructures as the specific failure of prior generators. Component-counting criteria reward the presence of both parts; only the obstacle tells you whether the combination was work.

proposals.name: Abstract bulk: length, sentence count, paragraph count
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how BULKY the abstract is as a piece of text. 0 = very short (roughly one short paragraph, under about 100 words, only a handful of sentences); 5 = one substantial paragraph of moderate length; 10 = very long and multi-paragraph (several hundred words, many sentences, two or more paragraph breaks). Estimate word count, sentence count and number of paragraph breaks and score from those alone; do not read for content. You must NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether more text means more content, whether the writing is efficient, or whether a long abstract is better or worse than a short one. Score only the extent of textual bulk.
proposals.rationale: Sheer text volume gives any criterion-checking reader more explicit surface to match against, independent of merit: a longer abstract mentions more things and therefore satisfies more separately written criteria. In this slice the shortest items sit on the dense_high_card_low arm - R21 is three sentences, R53 and R07 are single short paragraphs, and R50, R14, R38 and R60 are barely longer - while the bulkiest items sit on the dense_low_card_high arm: R32 runs a multi-paragraph bulleted body, and R44, R36, R25, R29, R13 and R55 all run several hundred words. Word count is not research quality; R07 and R21 each state a complete contribution in a few lines.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Public-release and link boilerplate (code, data, project page)
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text contains explicit availability or release statements: full URLs (GitHub repositories, project pages, university or lab sites, shortened links), and phrases such as 'code is available', 'publicly available', 'we release', 'our data and code can be found at', 'model weights are public', 'see our project page'. 0 = no availability statement and no URL anywhere; 5 = a bare availability phrase with no location; 10 = multiple release statements and one or more full URLs, prominently placed. Score only the presence, count and prominence of release/availability language. You must NOT judge whether releasing artifacts is good practice, whether the release seems credible or complete, whether the work looks reproducible, or whether the hosting location seems reputable.
proposals.rationale: A pasted URL is a single cheap token that any criterion bank can reward, yet it reflects whether a group has spare engineering hands and a habit of shipping, not what was discovered. The asymmetry across the two arms of this slice is stark: nearly every dense_low_card_high item carries a link or a release sentence (R01, R02, R13, R15, R17, R25, R33, R46, R54, R55), while the most extreme dense_high_card_low items carry neither (R21, R53, R07, R50, R38, R60). Tagged mixed because groups with the capacity to release code plausibly also do more careful work, so the discount should be reported as a band rather than assumed to be pure nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: the producing group's release norms and its engineering or staffing capacity to package artifacts

proposals.name: Itemized contribution inventory (First/Second/Third, numbered lists)
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how heavily the text is ITEMIZED. Count explicit enumerators ('First,', 'Second,', 'Thirdly', 'Firstly', 'Finally', 'Next,'), parenthesized numerals such as '(1) ... (2) ...', roman or letter enumerators 'i) ... ii) ...' and '(a) ... (b) ...', bullet or dash glyphs beginning lines, and any announced count of contributions ('three major technical contributions', 'two complementary contributions', 'two intriguing properties'). 0 = continuous prose with no enumeration markers at all; 5 = one or two enumerators embedded in prose; 10 = an explicitly counted, fully itemized list structure with three or more marked items. Count the markers; do not assess whether the listed items are substantive or distinct. You must NOT judge whether itemizing is good writing, whether the contributions are worthwhile, or whether the count is honest.
proposals.rationale: Itemization makes each claim separately visible and separately countable, so an itemized abstract can tick more written criteria than an equally strong abstract that says the same things in prose. In this slice itemization concentrates on the dense_low_card_high arm: R44 announces 'three major technical contributions' and then runs First/Second/Third, R32 is a literal three-bullet list, R03 runs Firstly/Then/Finally, R06 labels '(1) Efficacy' and '(2) Retention', and R45 runs First/Second/Finally. The strongly non-itemized prose items sit opposite (R53, R42, R09, R21). Formatting a claim as numbered item three does not make it true or important, so this must never be a criterion.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Markup and PDF-extraction residue in the text
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the amount of raw markup and extraction debris visible in the text. Count: unrendered LaTeX commands written with a leading backslash (textit, texttt, url, emph, escaped percent signs); inline math source in dollar signs; markdown asterisk bold or italic; TeX-style opening/closing quote pairs of the form ``...''; bullet glyphs; stray braces or a link that has been broken in half; mid-word hyphenation left behind by line breaking (for example 'sur- rounding', 'uncer- tainty', 'ubiq- uitous', 'rigor- ous'); and hard line wrapping in the middle of sentences. 0 = clean rendered prose with none of this; 5 = a few isolated artifacts; 10 = pervasive residue throughout. Count artifacts only. You must NOT judge whether the residue looks sloppy, unprofessional, hurried or careless, and you must not let its presence colour any impression of the work.
proposals.rationale: This is entirely a property of the typesetting and scraping pipeline - which macros survived conversion, where the PDF happened to wrap a line - and is causally disconnected from the research. It is unevenly distributed across this slice and therefore acts as a silent covariate on any text-only reader: R06 carries markdown bold and 'sur- rounding', R32 carries bullet glyphs plus 'ubiq- uitous' and 'rigor- ous', R26 carries 'uncer- tainty', R14 carries a TeX-quoted ``agnostic'', R15 carries backslash-textit and backslash-url, R55 carries backslash-texttt, R33 ends with a link broken across a stray brace, and R25 is hard-wrapped mid-sentence throughout.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Visible compute, data and paid-annotation scale markers
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text foregrounds large compute or large resources. Count mentions of: named large hardware (TPU pods, A100, A6000, 'GPU hours', 'multiple performant GPUs', 'inside a single GPU'); very large parameter, batch, dataset or sample counts (175 billion parameters, batch size in the tens of thousands, billions of parameters, hundreds of thousands of collected pairs, tens of thousands of curated questions); large-scale corpora and benchmark suites (ImageNet-scale training, web-scale text corpora); paid or organised human annotation (crowdworker studies, hired expert annotators, large human evaluation); and artifact URLs that identify a large institution or corporate lab. 0 = no resource or scale markers; 10 = several prominent ones. Score only how visible resource markers are in the wording. You must NOT judge whether the scale is impressive, necessary, well spent, or whether large-scale evidence is stronger evidence.
proposals.rationale: Who could afford the run is an unseen upstream factor, but it leaves a loud and directly scorable fingerprint in the wording. R13 names 175 billion parameters, four GPU hours, A100 and A6000; R35 names a TPUv3 Pod and a batch size of 32868; R05 gives a corporate-lab research URL and a paid crowdworker preference study; R34 reports 850K collected instruction pairs; R27 pushes network depth to ResNet-638 at ImageNet scale; R36 reports 18K curated questions over 28 evaluated models. This phrasing is available to a well-funded lab whether or not the underlying idea is good, so it cannot be a merit criterion. Tagged mixed because compute genuinely does enable more thorough evidence.
proposals.upstream_parent: the producing group's compute budget, funding level and institutional affiliation

proposals.name: Playful, idiomatic or pop-culture title register
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how playful or colloquial the register of the TITLE is. Look for: puns and wordplay, alliteration, nursery-rhyme or pop-culture allusion, imperative or second-person phrasing addressed to the reader, jokey or self-deprecating self-description, scare-quoted words, and titles that read as a spoken sentence or slogan rather than a technical noun phrase. 0 = a plain descriptive technical noun phrase; 5 = a conventional title with one mildly informal flourish; 10 = an overtly jokey, idiomatic or slogan-like title. Judge the register of the wording only. You must NOT judge whether the title is effective, memorable, apt, or tasteful, and you must not infer anything about how serious or careful the work behind it is.
proposals.rationale: Informal titling is a social license rather than a writing choice: it is disproportionately taken up by authors established enough to feel they can risk it, which is precisely an unseen upstream factor that the title makes visible in text. Every clearly playful title in this slice falls on the same arm, dense_high_card_low: R28 'Hungry Hungry Hippos', R26 'VariBAD: A Very Good Method for Bayes-Adaptive Deep RL', R08 'Keep Doing What Worked', R60 'Fix your classifier: the marginal value of training the last weight layer', and R27 'Intriguing Properties of Adversarial Training at Scale'. Whether an author felt free to make a joke is not evidence about the research. Tagged mixed because the same standing that licenses the joke may also come with better research.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's standing and practice in this format - the social confidence to be informal in a competitive venue

proposals.name: Inline author-year citations and named-lineage continuation
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the abstract itself cites prior work by AUTHOR NAME AND YEAR inline - forms such as '(Surname & Surname, 2015)', 'cf. Surname et al. 2022', '(Surname, 1972; Surname, 1972)' - and the extent to which it names a specific prior method or framework as the direct thing being continued, corrected or improved ('a modern form of X called EF21 (Surname et al, 2021)', 'we leverage the framework of Surname et al. (2019)', 'improves the best-known theory of that method'). 0 = no named-author citations and no named predecessor method; 5 = one named predecessor or one inline citation; 10 = several inline author-year citations plus an explicit continuation of a named prior line. Count citation markers and named-lineage phrases. You must NOT judge whether the citations are apt, whether the cited lineage is prestigious, whether the positioning is honest, or whether citing in an abstract is good practice.
proposals.rationale: Author-year citations inside an abstract are a house style of people writing from inside an established thread - often their own thread - so the feature reports who is speaking rather than what was found. In this slice it clusters on the dense_high_card_low arm: R14 closes with 'cf. Mallinar et al. 2022', R31 cites Gibson 2017, Blahut 1972, Arimoto 1972 and Balle et al. 2021, R42 cites Frankle, Gur-Ari and Achille in a single sentence, and R57 cites Seide 2014 alongside three separate Richtarik entries while explicitly extending that same line. R32 shows the identical style on the opposite arm, confirming it is a stylistic covariate rather than a merit measure. Tagged mixed because deeply embedded authors may also produce stronger work.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's embeddedness and seniority within a specific research lineage, frequently continuing their own prior line

proposals.name: Non-idiomatic English and unedited-prose irregularities
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the frequency of non-idiomatic or unpolished English in the text. Count: missing or superfluous articles; subject-verb or singular/plural disagreement; wrong verb form after a preposition (for example 'aims to establishing'); odd collocations and near-miss word choices (for example 'regarding with', a mechanism that 'stimulates' a strategy where 'emulates' is meant, 'grave limitations'); abrupt or non-standard connective openings ('But,' beginning a sentence, 'Moreover,' chains); and long multiply-embedded clauses that must be re-read to parse. 0 = uniformly idiomatic, fluent, evidently copy-edited prose; 5 = occasional irregularities; 10 = frequent irregularities throughout. Score only how often such surface irregularities occur. You must NOT judge whether the writing is good, whether the authors seem careless, whether the ideas come across clearly, or whether fluent prose indicates a better paper.
proposals.rationale: Language background and whether anyone edited the draft are unseen upstream factors that leave a direct, easily detectable textual trace while saying nothing about the science. The trace is clearly present and graded in this slice: R51 has 'aims to establishing node-wise correspondence' and 'regarding with matching accuracy' and sits at the extreme low end of the card arm, R40 has 'which we postulate is not ideal' and 'has received inadequate attention' and sits there too, while R24 opens a sentence with 'But,' and R10 speaks of 'two grave limitations' on the opposite arm. Because the irregularities appear on both arms it is a live confound that can pull either reader, which is exactly what a declared nuisance is for. Tagged mixed because access to editing correlates with better-resourced environments that may also support better research.
proposals.upstream_parent: the authors' first language and their access to copy-editing or writing assistance

proposals.name: Era-marker vocabulary dating the submission cohort
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how strongly the vocabulary dates the text to the most recent research cohort rather than to an earlier one. Recent markers: 'large language models' or 'LLM', 'agents' and 'agentic', 'multimodal' or 'LMM', 'foundation model', 'diffusion model', 'prompt' and 'promptable', 'hallucination', 'context-faithfulness', 'role-playing', 'AI-generated content', 'synthetic data detection', and named recent systems. Older markers: batch normalization, GANs, BERT probing, meta-reinforcement-learning, learned Bloom filters, ImageNet classification accuracy, ResNet variants, lottery-ticket and early-training framings, kernel ridge regression. 0 = vocabulary characteristic of the older cohort; 5 = mixed or period-neutral vocabulary; 10 = vocabulary characteristic of the newest cohort. Score the period of the vocabulary only. You must NOT judge whether the topic is important, timely, fashionable or dated, and you must not reward or penalise the subject matter itself.
proposals.rationale: When a submission was written is unseen, but it is heavily fingerprinted by topic vocabulary, and any reader fitted on a period-skewed pool will track that fingerprint rather than merit. The two arms of this slice differ visibly in period composition: LLM, agent and multimodal items concentrate on the dense_low_card_high arm (R03 proactive LLM agents, R06 self-updatable LLMs, R17 LLM knowledge fusion, R22 factuality versus context-faithfulness, R36 an LMM synthetic-data benchmark, R44 personality neurons in LLMs), while older-cohort topics concentrate on the dense_high_card_low arm (R07 learned Bloom filters, R21 the 2-simplicial Transformer, R42 the early phase of training, R60 fixing the last weight layer, R09 generalization error across scales). A paper is not better for having been written later. Tagged mixed because later work does stand on more prior progress.
proposals.upstream_parent: the year and submission cohort in which the item was written

proposals.name: Late-entrant positioning inside an already-crowded thread
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how strongly the text presents itself as arriving LATE into an already-busy line of work rather than opening one. Late-entrant fingerprints: survey-like openers such as 'Various methods have been devised', 'A line of research has made some progress', 'Recently, X was proposed ... however', 'existing works either ... or ...', 'most prior methods fail'; an inventory of several named recent competitors that the contribution is measured against; and a contribution framed as a fix, extension, refinement or drop-in plug-in to a named predecessor. Line-opening fingerprints: the problem is set up from first principles with few or no named recent rivals; the contribution is framed as a first framing, a first attempt, or the introduction of a new object. 0 = clearly line-opening; 5 = ordinary related-work framing; 10 = clearly a late entrant crowded in behind many named predecessors. Score only how the text positions itself in the sequence of comparable work. You must NOT judge whether arriving early or late is better, whether the claimed delta is large, or whether the novelty is real.
proposals.rationale: The item's actual position in the stream is unobservable, but it dictates the rhetoric it must adopt: whoever writes the twentieth entry on a topic has to enumerate the nineteen before it, while whoever writes the first does not, so the position leaves a scorable textual trace. The split is visible here. Late-entrant phrasing marks dense_low_card_high items - R01 opens 'Various methods have been devised' and then 'Recently, weight balancing ... has been proposed', R11 argues that 'most knowledge distillation methods ... have failed', R55 measures itself against AdvCaT and YOLOv8, R41 slots itself among several named anti-collapse methods. Line-opening phrasing marks dense_high_card_low items - R07 says 'Here we show how to frame the problem', R21 simply says 'We introduce the 2-simplicial Transformer', R31 says it 'makes the first attempt at an algorithm' for its problem. Tagged mixed because being early in a thread can genuinely mean the contribution is more original, so the parent plausibly causes real quality as well as favourable reception.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream - how many comparable entries preceded this one and how crowded its container was

proposals.name: Single unifying insight vs. contribution checklist
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract is organized around one clear, unifying finding versus a loose bundle of separate contributions. A 10 is an abstract whose every sentence supports a single central claim or mechanism, with no independent side-contributions. A 0 is an abstract that enumerates three or more loosely related fixes/contributions (e.g. numbered 'First...Second...Third' or 'three technical contributions') that could each stand alone with no unifying thread connecting them.
proposals.rationale: R21 (dense_pct=0.999) and R55 (dense_pct=0.707) each build toward one crisp claim in a short space and score high with the dense model; R39 (card_pct=0.997, three separate DNC problems each with its own fix) and R28 (card_pct=0.994, explicitly 'three major technical contributions') pad out list-like abstracts that the scorecard rates far above the dense model.

proposals.name: Explains causal mechanism, not just reports outcome
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract explains WHY an effect occurs (a causal or mechanistic account) rather than only reporting THAT something improved. A 10 gives a specific causal hypothesis or mechanism for an observed phenomenon. A 0 states an outcome (faster, smaller, higher accuracy) with no account of the underlying reason it happens.
proposals.rationale: R59 (dense_pct=0.920) proposes a 'two-domain hypothesis' explaining why batch norm hurts adversarial robustness, and R36 (dense_pct=0.916) explains robustness gaps via a new label-uncertainty account -- both dense-favored; R06 (card_pct=0.946, InfinityGAN) and R14 (card_pct=0.842, Colorization Transformer) describe multi-step pipelines and report quality gains without explaining why the pipeline choices produce those gains.

proposals.name: Formal rigor: proof or derived bound anchors the claim
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the presence of a formal theoretical result (theorem, proof, derived bound, convergence guarantee) that is central -- not decorative -- to the paper's claim. A 10 is built around an explicit proved/derived result. A 0 is purely empirical with no formal analysis of any kind.
proposals.rationale: R07 (dense_pct=0.979) derives the first sandwich-bound algorithm for general sources, R11 (dense_pct=0.935) proves an arithmetic- vs quadratic-mean improvement, and R55 (dense_pct=0.707) extends the Gauss-Markov theorem -- all dense-favored; R42 (card_pct=0.815) and R50 (card_pct=0.989) are pure empirical/benchmark reports with no derived formal claim, yet the scorecard rates them far higher than the dense model does.

proposals.name: Avoids generic promotional/hype boilerplate language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on freedom from generic hype phrasing ('remarkable', 'significant interest', 'paves the way', 'increasingly proficient', 'extensive experiments validate the efficacy') that could be pasted into almost any paper regardless of its actual content. A 10 states the contribution plainly with no boilerplate framing. A 0 opens or closes with generic motivational language disconnected from the specific technical finding.
proposals.rationale: R21 (dense_pct=0.999) and R23 (dense_pct=0.712) state their contribution directly with zero hype framing; R35 (card_pct=0.956, 'remarkable abilities...paving the way for future advancements') and R28 (card_pct=0.994, 'increasingly proficient...Extensive experiments validates the efficacy') lean heavily on generic promotional phrasing while scoring far higher on the scorecard than on the dense model.

proposals.name: Shows removable complexity: simpler solution suffices
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's central finding is that some previously assumed-necessary complexity can be removed or simplified without loss (an ablation/reduction insight). A 10 explicitly shows a component, stage, or assumption is unnecessary. A 0 only adds new machinery/components with no such simplification finding.
proposals.rationale: R52 (dense_pct=0.889, 'only a very few modern components are critical...many others are nonessential') and R24 (dense_pct=0.928, classifier weights can be fixed 'with little or no loss of accuracy') both earn a strong simplification finding and score high with the dense model; by contrast R06 (card_pct=0.946) and R39 (card_pct=0.997) add successive machinery/fixes rather than removing any, yet score far higher on the scorecard.

proposals.name: Stays tightly scoped, no bonus-application padding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract stays tightly scoped to one well-defined technical claim versus tacking on a list of loosely related 'extra applications' or bonus demonstrations to inflate perceived scope. A 10 stays focused on the core claim start to finish. A 0 appends a list of separate bonus use-cases (e.g. 'style fusing, outpainting, and inbetweening') that are not needed to support the core claim.
proposals.rationale: R23 (dense_pct=0.712) and R55 (dense_pct=0.707) stay tightly scoped to a single framing/theorem; R06 (card_pct=0.946) appends 'fusing styles spatially, multi-modal outpainting, and image inbetweening' as bonus applications, and R29 (card_pct=0.960) tacks on a downstream recognition-boosting application plus a released benchmark, both scoring far above the dense model.

proposals.name: States a genuinely surprising, precisely contrasted finding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract reports a result that runs counter to a stated expectation or prior consensus, expressed with a crisp, specific contrast (not a vague 'surprisingly'). A 10 gives a precise counterintuitive contrast (e.g. 'error regions have much higher X than randomly-selected regions'). A 0 reports an expected, incremental improvement with no counterintuitive twist.
proposals.rationale: R59 (dense_pct=0.920, an 'unexpected observation' that removing clean images boosts robustness 18.3%) and R36 (dense_pct=0.916, error regions have 'much higher label uncertainty than randomly-selected subsets') both land precise surprising contrasts and score high with the dense model, while R01 (card_pct=0.766) and R14 (card_pct=0.842) report expected, incremental engineering gains yet score far higher on the scorecard.

proposals.name: Primary contribution is understanding, not a new benchmark artifact
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's primary contribution is new scientific/technical understanding versus a new benchmark, dataset, or leaderboard artifact being the headline deliverable. A 10 centers on an insight or characterization. A 0 centers on 'we introduce a new benchmark/dataset of N items' as the first-listed contribution.
proposals.rationale: R30 (dense_pct=0.959) and R49 (dense_pct=0.807) are pure phenomenon-characterization papers with no new dataset; R50 (card_pct=0.989, 'we introduce LOKI, a novel benchmark...18K carefully curated questions'), R28 (card_pct=0.994, 'we construct PERSONALITYBENCH, a large-scale dataset' as its first contribution), and R35 (card_pct=0.956, ProactiveBench '6,790 events') all lead with a benchmark/dataset artifact and score far higher on the scorecard than the dense model.

proposals.name: Mechanistic narrative over stacked disconnected percentage claims
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's evidence is carried by an explanatory narrative versus a string of disconnected numeric improvement claims across many baselines/settings with no unifying account. A 10 uses at most one or two numbers, each embedded in an explanatory narrative. A 0 strings together three or more standalone percentage/speedup numbers (over baseline A, over baseline B, over baseline C) as the primary evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: R21 (dense_pct=0.999) and R57 (dense_pct=0.989) carry their claims analytically with essentially no stacked benchmark numbers; R37 (card_pct=0.969, '3 or 4 bits...3.25x...4.5x') and R42 (card_pct=0.815, '92.7%...28.5%...49.5%') pile up disconnected numeric claims across settings and score far higher on the scorecard than the dense model.

proposals.name: Reframes the problem, not just combines existing techniques
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract reframes a known problem through a genuinely new conceptual lens or formalism versus merely combining two or more existing techniques to patch two separately-diagnosed issues. A 10 introduces a new way of conceiving the problem itself. A 0 pairs technique X with technique Y, each addressing a separately-named sub-problem, with no new unifying concept.
proposals.rationale: R23 (dense_pct=0.712) frames Bloom-filter model utilization as an optimization problem, and R33 (dense_pct=0.982) frames the model-based/model-free RL tradeoff as a Bayesian posterior lower bound -- both genuine reframings; R27 (card_pct=0.899, 'attention-guided distillation AND non-local distillation' addressing two separately-diagnosed causes) and R08 (card_pct=0.955, importing a cognitive-science method and applying it to CLIP) combine existing pieces without introducing a new unifying concept, yet score far higher on the scorecard.

proposals.name: Central finding is a trade-off or negative result
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's central contribution is a trade-off, failure mode, or negative/mixed result rather than a new method that outperforms prior work. A 10 centers entirely on demonstrating a limitation or trade-off. A 0 centers entirely on a positive method with a clean win over baselines.
proposals.rationale: R19 (card_pct=0.957) centers on showing factuality enhancement 'can significantly undermine context-faithfulness' (a striking 69.7% decline) with no new winning method proposed, and R09 (card_pct=0.886) centers on networks being 'unable to generalize' to a logic task even after targeted training; both are trade-off/negative-result papers that the scorecard rates far above where the dense model places them.

proposals.name: Grounds central concept in a non-ML theoretical framework
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's central concept is explicitly grounded in an established theoretical framework from outside mainstream ML (linguistics, cognitive science, causal inference, psychology) with named provenance, versus being framed purely in ML-internal terms. A 10 explicitly imports and cites a non-ML framework as the basis for its central definition. A 0 uses only ML-internal architectural/empirical framing.
proposals.rationale: R05 (card_pct=0.942) explicitly draws 'on principles from traditional linguistics' to define implicitness, R08 (card_pct=0.955) imports 'methodological tools from the cognitive science literature' (picture-word interference), and R13 (card_pct=0.981) argues 'the language of causality offers clarity' for defining spuriousness -- all three import outside theoretical frameworks and are rated far higher by the scorecard than by the dense model.

proposals.name: Explains an existing phenomenon vs. names a new system
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's primary contribution is characterizing/explaining an already-observed phenomenon versus introducing a new named architecture, model, or system as the headline deliverable. A 10 is a pure analysis/characterization paper with no new named system. A 0 leads with a new named model/system as the headline contribution.
proposals.rationale: R30 (dense_pct=0.959, 'Phenomenology of Double Descent') and R49 (dense_pct=0.807, 'The Early Phase of Neural Network Training') are pure characterization papers introducing no new named system, both dense-favored; R06 (card_pct=0.946, InfinityGAN) and R20 (card_pct=0.789, SELF-PARAM) each lead with a new named system as the headline, and both score far higher on the scorecard than on the dense model.

proposals.name: High content-to-preamble ratio; minimal throat-clearing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the fraction of the abstract spent on the actual technical contribution versus generic motivational/context-setting preamble before the contribution is introduced. A 10 begins stating the actual contribution within the first sentence or two. A 0 spends multiple sentences on generic field-level motivation ('X has attracted widespread attention', 'X remains a substantial challenge') before any specific contribution appears.
proposals.rationale: R21 (dense_pct=0.999) opens directly with 'We introduce the 2-simplicial Transformer...' with zero preamble, and R23 (dense_pct=0.712) reaches its contribution within two sentences; R35 (card_pct=0.956) and R50 (card_pct=0.989, 'garnered widespread attention...attracted significant interest') both spend several sentences on generic field-level scene-setting before reaching their specific contribution, yet score far higher on the scorecard.

proposals.name: Each added mechanism specifically described and individually justified
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the combination of (a) how mechanistically specific the description of each technical component is (not just named, but explained in terms of what it computes) together with (b) whether each added component/stage carries its own stated justification for being necessary. A 10 describes every moving part concretely and explains why each one is needed. A 0 names components generically ('we propose a module for X') and, when there are multiple components, gives no individual justification for why each is needed beyond 'this improves performance'.
proposals.rationale: R60 (dense_pct=0.722) specifies its mechanism precisely ('an energy function directly extracted from a graph neural network trained with standard supervised classification loss') and R33 (dense_pct=0.982) ties each design choice to a stated reason (trading off model-free/model-based estimates 'according to their epistemic uncertainties' to enable conservatism); by contrast R39 (card_pct=0.997) lists three fixes for three problems with only the generic claim they 'yield improved performance', and R17 (card_pct=0.780) describes its fusion mechanism vaguely ('leveraging the generative distributions of source LLMs, we externalize their collective knowledge') -- both scoring far higher on the scorecard than the dense model despite this vagueness.

proposals.name: Abstract length/verbosity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how long and verbose this abstract is relative to a typical ML conference abstract (0 = extremely terse, only a few short sentences; 10 = unusually long, with many sentences and clauses). Score only the extent of length/verbosity present in the text; do not judge whether the length is appropriate or whether the paper itself is good.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R34 run to many long, clause-dense sentences covering multiple sub-results, while R13 and R26 are two-to-five sentence abstracts stating a single idea; length/verbosity varies across both disagreement directions (R08 is dense_high, R34 is dense_low) so it is plausibly predictive of how a text-only reader scores the item independent of the underlying research content.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Raw markup/LaTeX leakage
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much uncompiled markup or LaTeX source leaks into the visible text (e.g., literal double-asterisk bold markers, \texttt{...}, \url{...} remnants, stray braces, bullet characters like '•', or duplicated/broken links). 0 = clean prose with no markup artifacts; 10 = heavy visible markup debris. Score only the presence of these typographic artifacts, not whether the underlying formatting choice was a good one.
proposals.rationale: R51 leaves literal '**Efficacy**' and '**Retention**' bold markers uncompiled; R39's abstract ends with a visibly broken, duplicated link '...GEnBP}{github.com/danmackinlay/GEnBP'; R28 shows raw '\texttt{UV-Attack}'; R30 uses raw '•' bullet characters. This is a submission-pipeline/rendering artifact unrelated to the underlying research.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Code/model/data public-release boilerplate
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how explicitly the text states that code, data, models, or checkpoints have been or will be publicly released (e.g., 'code is available at...', 'Codes have been released on Github', a repo/project-page URL). 0 = no such statement anywhere; 10 = a prominent, explicit release statement with a link. Score only whether this boilerplate sentence/link is present, not whether releasing code is a good practice or reflects a strong paper.
proposals.rationale: R21 ('Codes have been released on Github'), R59 ('code and pre-trained checkpoints... are publicly available'), and R37 (github link) all carry this exact boilerplate; groups with a habitual open-sourcing practice may also tend to write more complete, careful abstracts, so the parent factor is plausibly entangled with genuine rigor as well as being a pure stylistic habit.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's/lab's standing habit of open-sourcing artifacts (a submission norm shaped by lab culture or subfield convention, not by the idea itself)

proposals.name: Self-reported numeric win-margin density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how many explicit numeric superiority claims over baselines appear in the abstract (specific percentages, point deltas, or multiplicative speedups, e.g., '43.9 AP, which is 4.1 higher', '92.7% ASR', '3.25x speedup'). 0 = no such figures; 10 = the abstract is dense with several such headline numbers. Score only the count/density of these figures, not whether the reported improvement is actually meaningful, correct, or well-measured.
proposals.rationale: R28 stacks three such figures ('92.7%... 28.5%... 49.5%'), R21 states '43.9 AP...4.1 higher than the baseline', and R37 states '3.25x' and '4.5x' speedups; this habit could also correlate with genuinely more thorough empirical validation, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's/venue's benchmark-competition submission culture (a rhetorical habit of leading with SOTA-beating numbers, distinct from the underlying contribution)

proposals.name: Named-prior-method competitive density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how many distinct named prior systems or baselines the abstract explicitly claims to outperform (e.g., 'MOPO', 'MOReL', 'COMBO', 'LARS', 'AdvCaT'). 0 = no named baselines mentioned; 10 = the abstract names and reports beating many distinct prior systems. Score only the count of named-baseline comparisons present, not whether the comparison is fair, apples-to-apples, or convincing.
proposals.rationale: R50 names and quantifies wins over 'MOPO', 'MOReL' and 'COMBO'; R49 names 'LARS' as the incumbent it improves on; R28 names 'AdvCaT' as the state-of-the-art it surpasses; density of named rivals tracks subfield crowdedness rather than the intrinsic merit of the new idea, though thorough benchmarking can also reflect real rigor.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's engagement with an already-crowded, fast-moving competitive subfield (how many prior 'obvious' approaches had already been staked out by named competitors by the time this entry was written)

proposals.name: New-benchmark/dataset scale statistics
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract quantifies the scale of a NEW benchmark, dataset, or evaluation suite it introduces (explicit counts such as '18K questions', '26 subcategories', '6,790 events', 'evaluated 22 open-source and 6 closed-source models'). 0 = no such scale statistics; 10 = the abstract is full of precise scale numbers for a new resource. Score only the presence/density of these resource-scale statistics, not whether the resource is well-designed or useful.
proposals.rationale: R34 reports '18K carefully curated questions across 26 subcategories' and evaluation of '22 open-source LMMs and 6 closed-source models'; R47 reports 'ProactiveBench, containing 6,790 events' plus human-annotator labeling; this scale signal could also enable genuinely more rigorous evaluation, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: team size and annotation/engineering budget behind the submission (larger benchmark-construction efforts typically require bigger teams, compute, or crowd-labeling budgets)

proposals.name: Named industrial-scale compute/model infrastructure
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract name-drops specific large-scale industrial compute hardware or very large named pretrained model families (e.g., 'TPUv3 Pod', 'NVIDIA A100', '175 billion parameters', 'Llama-2', 'MPT', 'OpenLLaMA'). 0 = no such mentions; 10 = multiple specific large-scale infrastructure/model names appear. Score only the presence of these named-infrastructure mentions, not whether using them was necessary, impressive, or led to a good result.
proposals.rationale: R49 references training 'to the memory limit of a TPUv3 Pod'; R37 references '175 billion parameters', 'NVIDIA A100', and 'NVIDIA A6000'; R45 names 'Llama-2, MPT, and OpenLLaMA' as the fused base models; this resourcing tell could also correlate with genuinely larger, more convincing experiments.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's institutional access to industrial-scale compute resources (large industry lab vs. smaller academic group)

proposals.name: Contemporary LLM/agent-era vocabulary density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of the abstract's vocabulary belongs to the current large-language-model/agent wave (terms like 'large language models', 'hallucination', 'context-faithfulness', 'agents', 'in-context', 'proactive', 'self-updatable') as opposed to classical statistical/ML-theory vocabulary. 0 = no such terms present; 10 = the abstract is saturated with this vocabulary. Score only the density of this topical vocabulary, not whether the topic choice itself is a good or important one.
proposals.rationale: R32 is built entirely around 'large language models', 'hallucinations', and 'context-faithfulness'; R47's title and body foreground 'Proactive Agent' and 'LLM Agents'; contrast with R18's 'kernel ridge regression (KRR)' or R43's 'Gauss-Markov theorem', which use timeless statistical-learning vocabulary with none of these terms; topical fashion could also track genuine current relevance, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing / which topical wave of the conference cycle the paper was written in

proposals.name: Rhetorical challenge to a stated prior consensus
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how explicitly the abstract frames itself as challenging, questioning, or overturning an already-established prior consensus or narrative (phrases like 'There is a consensus that...', 'Is X a free lunch?', 'an open secret', 'despite alarm over...'). 0 = no such framing, the contribution is presented on its own terms; 10 = the abstract is structured explicitly around rebutting a named consensus. Score only whether this rhetorical structure is present, not whether the challenge is correct, novel, or well-argued.
proposals.rationale: R14 opens 'There is a consensus that such poisons can hardly harm adversarially-trained (AT) models...' before challenging it; R32's title is literally 'Is Factuality Enhancement a Free Lunch For LLMs?'; R56 opens 'An open secret in contemporary machine learning is...'; R24 opens 'Despite alarm over the reliance of machine learning systems on so-called spurious patterns...' — all stage themselves as a rebuttal to a named prior view rather than a freestanding first framing.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the run of the field — this framing is only available to an entry written after a prior 'obvious' consensus view has already been staked out and named by others

proposals.name: Recency/citation-stream density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract explicitly situates itself within a recent wave of related work, via words like 'recent(ly)', 'recent studies/advances/work', or inline dated citations (e.g., '(Frankle et al., 2019)'). 0 = no recency or citation markers, reads as a self-contained, foundational framing; 10 = the abstract is dense with recency language and/or multiple inline dated citations. Score only the density of these markers, not whether the cited prior work is correctly or fairly characterized.
proposals.rationale: R17 opens 'Recent studies have shown...' and packs in three inline dated citations, '(Frankle et al., 2019)', '(Gur-Ari et al., 2018)', and '(Achille et al., 2019)'; R56 opens 'recent advances in generative adversarial networks (GANs) suggest otherwise'; R52 opens 'Recent studies have presented compelling evidence...'; density of this framing could also reflect genuinely thorough literature grounding, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream — how late, relative to a cluster of closely related prior work, this item was written, i.e., how many 'obvious' recent takes it is explicitly responding to

proposals.name: Bottleneck–mechanism alignment
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract identifies a specific bottleneck and each main design choice directly addresses it; give 0 when the method is presented without a concrete problem-to-mechanism link.
proposals.rationale: R01, R10, R25, and R32 each connect a diagnosed failure mode to a tailored architectural or algorithmic response.

proposals.name: Explanatory mechanism depth
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the work explains why a phenomenon occurs using a coherent mechanism, theory, or diagnostic analysis; give 0 when it mainly reports a method and aggregate empirical gains without explanation.
proposals.rationale: R05, R20, R21, and R45 investigate underlying representation, robustness, or training dynamics rather than only introducing a technique.

proposals.name: Causal intervention validation
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract describes targeted manipulations, ablations, or controlled comparisons that test a proposed cause; give 0 when no evidence isolates which factor produced the claimed behavior.
proposals.rationale: R17 analyzes specific DNC failure modes before proposing fixes, while R44 and R55 deconstruct components to test their individual roles.

proposals.name: Boundary-condition honesty
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract states assumptions, limitations, failure modes, or trade-offs and confines claims accordingly; give 0 when it makes broad unconditional claims with no stated scope.
proposals.rationale: R02 qualifies its theoretical setting, R15 reports failures to generalize, R27 identifies a factuality–faithfulness trade-off, and R48 states distributional assumptions.

proposals.name: Shift and scale transfer
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the method is tested across meaningful changes in data distribution, resolution, model architecture, task, or scale; give 0 when evidence is confined to one standard setting.
proposals.rationale: R14, R47, R55, and R59 explicitly examine unseen architectures, poses, robustness scales, or resolutions.

proposals.name: Controlled counterfactual testing
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when evaluation varies a targeted factor while preserving or clarifying the underlying task, enabling causal interpretation; give 0 when evaluation uses only undifferentiated benchmark variation.
proposals.rationale: R19 studies controlled visual transformations, R50 manipulates embedded language, R52 uses counterfactually revised text, and R27 separates contextual from parametric knowledge.

proposals.name: Structure-matched inductive bias
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the representation or architecture encodes a real structural property of the domain and the abstract explains why that structure matters; give 0 when the architecture is generic or structurally unmotivated.
proposals.rationale: R12 uses higher-order attention for logic, R51 uses hyperbolic geometry for hierarchies, and R59 uses finite-element structure for physical dynamics.

proposals.name: Coherent component composition
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when multiple components have complementary roles, explicit interfaces, and jointly address coupled failure modes; give 0 when the abstract lists loosely connected modules without explaining their interaction.
proposals.rationale: R03 combines H3 and FlashConv around memory and hardware limitations, while R04 and R25 coordinate perception, planning, navigation, and manipulation capabilities.

proposals.name: Theory-to-design usefulness
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when theoretical analysis directly yields an actionable algorithm, training rule, or diagnostic and the abstract connects it to experiments; give 0 when the formal result is detached from design implications.
proposals.rationale: R02 turns an equivalence result into a learning-rate interpretation, R13 converts sharper convergence analysis into EF21 variants, and R16 derives an online-distillation strategy.

proposals.name: Capability per resource
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract quantifies capability relative to computation, memory, training time, data, or model size under realistic constraints; give 0 when resource demands and savings are not addressed.
proposals.rationale: R07, R33, R41, and R49 explicitly connect model behavior to training time, inference hardware, memory, or parameter costs.

proposals.name: Necessary simplification
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the work removes components or assumptions while preserving or improving the target capability and explains why the simplification works; give 0 when it adds complexity without establishing necessity.
proposals.rationale: R44 shows that many diffusion components are unnecessary for representation learning, R49 fixes the classifier layer, and R32 presents a deliberately simple offline-RL solution.

proposals.name: Transferable abstraction
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the central insight or module is shown to transfer across tasks, domains, architectures, or existing methods; give 0 when it is tied to one bespoke configuration.
proposals.rationale: R26 presents reusable graph-matching components, R30 applies compression across NLP architectures and tasks, and R13 extends its analysis across distributed-training variants.

proposals.name: Construct-valid measurement
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when evaluation directly measures the intended scientific construct, separates nearby confounds, and uses appropriate human, expert, behavioral, or controlled validation; give 0 when a convenient proxy is weakly connected to the claim.
proposals.rationale: R15, R50, R56, and R40 design tests or metrics intended to distinguish logical reasoning, semantic interference, implicitness, or multimodal detection rather than relying on generic accuracy alone.

proposals.name: Actionable interpretability
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when analysis exposes internal structure that supports prediction, intervention, control, or a substantive scientific explanation and validates that use; give 0 when interpretability is only visualization or post hoc labeling.
proposals.rationale: R23 derives controllable hidden-state directions, R59 links learned components to physical dynamics, and R42 uses compositional prototypes to explain user interests.

proposals.name: Coverage of difficult regimes
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract deliberately targets rare, long-range, high-dimensional, sparse, or otherwise difficult cases and evaluates those cases explicitly; give 0 when it focuses only on average easy examples.
proposals.rationale: R01 addresses scarce labels and diverse 3D masks, R07 tests long-range hypergraph interactions, R36 emphasizes rare cuneiform signs, and R57 targets inference where ensemble size is far below state dimension.

proposals.name: Metric Saturation
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the abstract presents exact percentages, counts, time reductions, parameter sizes, or benchmark deltas; judge only the amount of numerical reporting, not whether the numbers are good or indicate research quality.
proposals.rationale: Dense quantitative packaging may attract attention while reflecting reporting convention rather than research quality. It is visible in R07, R18, and R21.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in conference abstract reporting

proposals.name: Acronym Branding
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the abstract uses coined method names, memorable acronyms, stylized capitalization, or branded project labels; judge only naming prominence, not whether the method is good or high quality.
proposals.rationale: Memorable labels can improve recall and processing independently of substance. This pattern appears in R05, R18, R48, and R60.
proposals.upstream_parent: community and venue naming conventions

proposals.name: Reproducibility Signaling
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of visible code, data, model, checkpoint, project-page, or public-availability claims; judge only the presence and prominence of these signals, not whether the work is reproducible or good.
proposals.rationale: Artifact signaling can affect reader trust while remaining a presentation and resource-availability cue rather than intrinsic quality. It appears in R06, R14, and R49.
proposals.upstream_parent: author or research-group practice regarding public artifacts

proposals.name: Citation Texture
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the amount of visible citation texture, including named prior papers, parenthetical references, historical attributions, and acronym-plus-author-year notation; judge only citation presence and density, not scholarly correctness or quality.
proposals.rationale: Citation style can cue field membership and credibility independently of the contribution's substance. Examples include R01, R03, and R19.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's disciplinary writing practice

proposals.name: Promotional Superlatives
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of superlative or promotional wording such as “first,” “remarkably,” “unprecedented,” “strikingly,” “superior,” or “opens the door”; judge only rhetorical intensity, not whether the claims are warranted or good.
proposals.rationale: Promotional language can change salience without measuring validity, originality, or evidential strength. It is visible in R08, R11, and R54.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission rhetoric and marketing style

proposals.name: Breadth Packaging
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the abstract enumerates many tasks, datasets, modalities, benchmarks, domains, or applications in one package; judge only the amount of enumeration, not whether the breadth is valuable or reflects quality.
proposals.rationale: A long list of evaluation settings can create an impression of scope while partly reflecting packaging strategy. This appears in R05, R30, and R45.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in packaging conference abstracts

proposals.name: Frontier-Topic Wording
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent to which the abstract relies on currently fashionable topic markers such as LLM, foundation model, diffusion, multimodal, adversarial, or embodied-agent language; judge only topic-word presence, not topic importance or research quality.
proposals.rationale: Topic salience can shape attention through community fashion without establishing the contribution's quality. The wording is prominent in R09, R22, and R54.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Formalism Density
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the amount of mathematical notation, named theoretical objects, norm symbols, equations, theorem language, and formal assumptions; judge only formalism density, not rigor, correctness, or quality.
proposals.rationale: Dense formal presentation can signal disciplinary familiarity and influence reading expectations without itself proving a sound contribution. Examples include R13, R26, and R51.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's mathematical communication and disciplinary style

proposals.name: Problem-Fix Template
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how strongly the abstract follows a limitation-to-remedy template using phrases such as “however,” “current methods,” “suffers from,” “to address,” and “we propose”; judge only the rhetorical structure, not whether the problem or fix is good.
proposals.rationale: A familiar problem-gap-solution structure can make an abstract easier to process while being independent of research quality. It appears in R07, R16, and R23.
proposals.upstream_parent: reviewer-facing abstract template

proposals.name: Late-Stream Differentiation Cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text reads like a response to an already crowded line of work, through repeated references to recent, existing, previous, standard, or competing approaches followed by a narrowly targeted distinction; judge only visible cues, not actual submission position, novelty, or quality.
proposals.rationale: A late-arriving entry may reflect awareness of established takes and additional revision time; those upstream conditions can affect presentation while not being research quality themselves. The fingerprint is visible in R07, R32, and R45.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream and submission timing

proposals.name: Failure-mode-to-mechanism fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a specific bottleneck and gives an intervention whose mechanism directly addresses it; score 0 when the method is generic or disconnected from the stated problem.
proposals.rationale: R07 links mobile skills to compounding navigation errors, while R42 links behavior priors to conflicting offline data sources.

proposals.name: Mechanistic explanatory depth
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract explains why a phenomenon occurs using formal analysis, targeted measurements, or component-level investigation; score 0 when it only proposes a method and reports aggregate results.
proposals.rationale: R04 analyzes early training changes through multiple measurements, and R28 systematically deconstructs diffusion models into contributing components.

proposals.name: Predictive transfer across regimes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract derives or tests predictions across unseen scales, resolutions, tasks, or domains using a stated mechanism; score 0 when evaluation remains confined to the development setting.
proposals.rationale: R05 predicts generalization across model and data scales, while R09 explicitly targets transfer to higher-resolution meshes.

proposals.name: Theory-method-experiment closure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal theory motivates a concrete method or hypothesis and experiments directly test its predictions; score 0 when theory, method, and experiments are presented as unrelated pieces.
proposals.rationale: R08 connects supervision-complexity theory to online distillation, and R59 develops an algorithm from a sharper communication-complexity analysis.

proposals.name: Boundary-condition stress testing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract deliberately evaluates varied, unseen, adversarial, black-box, or otherwise difficult conditions; score 0 when it tests only routine in-distribution conditions.
proposals.rationale: R24 tests unseen poses, views, and black-box detectors, while R31 examines higher budgets, partial poisoning, unseen architectures, and adaptive defenses.

proposals.name: Quantitative claim specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims are tied to concrete scales, budgets, assumptions, measurements, or comparative quantities; score 0 when the abstract relies mainly on vague adjectives without operational detail.
proposals.rationale: R17 specifies sequence lengths, model sizes, speedups, and perplexity gaps, while R21 gives parameter counts, bitwidths, runtime, and hardware settings.

proposals.name: Problem definition precision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract defines its target mathematically or operationally, distinguishes it from nearby concepts, and states what is measured; score 0 when it relies on broad labels without a precise object.
proposals.rationale: R13 formulates learned-filter utilization as an optimization problem, and R53 operationalizes implicitness as divergence between semantic meaning and pragmatic interpretation.

proposals.name: Domain-structure alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the architecture or objective explicitly encodes relevant geometry, hierarchy, physics, combinatorics, or compositional structure; score 0 when domain inputs are treated as generic feature vectors.
proposals.rationale: R09 builds on PDE and finite-element structure, while R58 uses chemically meaningful motifs and three-dimensional molecular constraints.

proposals.name: End-to-end practicality accounting
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract accounts for computation, memory, latency, data, or deployment constraints across the full workflow; score 0 when it claims efficiency without identifying the relevant bottlenecks.
proposals.rationale: R21 connects quantization to single-GPU execution and inference speed, while R60 relates optimization design to batch size, hardware limits, and training time.

proposals.name: Limitation and tradeoff awareness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract names failure modes, competing objectives, or unresolved limitations and analyzes them; score 0 when it presents only unqualified success claims.
proposals.rationale: R10 identifies dimensional collapse despite contrastive learning, and R37 analyzes the tradeoff between factuality and context-faithfulness.

proposals.name: Causal intervention quality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the study changes targeted factors or uses counterfactual controls to distinguish competing mechanisms; score 0 when it merely correlates observations with outcomes or compares opaque systems.
proposals.rationale: R04 contrasts labels with blurred inputs and auxiliary tasks, while R15 intervenes on clean/adversarial normalization and network depth.

proposals.name: Composable interface and reuse
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a contribution has clear inputs and outputs, can be inserted into existing systems, and its reuse conditions are explained; score 0 when it is inseparable from one monolithic pipeline.
