proposals.rationale: R01 explicitly presents its embedding and masking ideas as reusable plugins, while R07 decomposes long-horizon behavior into interacting mobile skills.

proposals.name: Evidence-set design validity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when datasets or tasks include meaningful controls, expert or human validation, broad variant coverage, and a direct connection to the claim; score 0 when evaluation data are narrow or weakly motivated.
proposals.rationale: R11 creates counterfactually paired documents with coherence and minimal-change requirements, while R56 combines expert annotations with rare and structurally varied signs.

proposals.name: Simplifying conceptual payoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work removes unnecessary components, stages, or learned machinery while preserving the intended function and explaining why; score 0 when it only adds complexity.
proposals.rationale: R28 reduces diffusion-based representation learning to a much simpler denoising formulation, while R48 simplifies a multi-stage long-tail method into one training stage.

proposals.name: Assumption and scope calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract states its assumptions, applicable regimes, and boundaries of interpretation; score 0 when it makes broad claims while leaving necessary assumptions implicit.
proposals.rationale: R02 distinguishes estimator formulas by norm and random-matrix setting, while R22 explicitly states its Gaussian-universality and agnostic-target assumptions.

proposals.name: Abstract verbosity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract is long, densely packed, or clause-heavy; judge only visible text and do not judge whether this verbosity is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Length and syntactic density may attract attention independently of research quality. This is visible in the extended, multi-stage presentations of R08 and R45.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Promotional novelty rhetoric
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text uses promotional, novelty, superlative, or attention-seeking wording; judge only its presence and not whether the claims are deserved.
proposals.rationale: Words such as "remarkably," "first," "striking," and "open secret" can influence reception without establishing quality. Examples include R13 and R50.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Public-release packaging
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract foregrounds code, data, models, project pages, URLs, or public availability; judge only the extent of this packaging and not whether the release is useful.
proposals.rationale: Authors experienced with conference conventions may routinely advertise reproducibility resources, and that practice may also accompany better work. Examples include R01 and R25.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Numerical result salience
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract foregrounds exact percentages, speedups, benchmark deltas, parameter counts, or other numerical results; judge only their prominence and not whether the results are impressive.
proposals.rationale: Numeric headlines are easy for readers or evaluators to notice and compare, regardless of underlying quality. Examples include R46 and R52.
proposals.upstream_parent: receiving-side preference for easily extractable evidence

proposals.name: Scope stacking
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract lists multiple tasks, datasets, domains, modalities, capabilities, or applications; judge only the breadth of the list and not whether the scope is valuable.
proposals.rationale: Broadly packaged projects may receive more attention, while ambitious teams may also produce genuinely strong research. Examples include R17 and R24.
proposals.upstream_parent: author or lab ambition and marketing practice

proposals.name: Formal-theory posture
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text emphasizes theorems, proofs, formal assumptions, bounds, derivations, or analytical guarantees; judge only the visible formal posture and not whether the mathematics is correct or important.
proposals.rationale: Theoretical framing can be favored by disciplinary norms and may also reflect real substantive sophistication. Examples include R16 and R21.
proposals.upstream_parent: field or community convention

proposals.name: Late-riff positioning
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract reads as a response, correction, reloading, extension, or contrast to an already-established line of work, using explicit gap and prior-work positioning; judge only this textual stance and not whether the response is justified.
proposals.rationale: A late-arriving entry may visibly frame itself against obvious earlier takes; additional iteration can also affect substantive work. Examples include the retrospective framing in R08 and the challenge-to-consensus framing in R48.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing and position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Editorial polish
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract exhibits smooth grammar, consistent terminology, regular formatting, and carefully edited prose; judge only presentation polish and not research quality.
proposals.rationale: Editing support or practiced abstract writing can improve perceived credibility without changing the underlying contribution. The polished prose and formatting of R12 and R39 illustrate this channel.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing or writing assistance

proposals.name: Contemporary fashion markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract uses currently fashionable topic labels, acronyms, and framing terms associated with prominent ML trends; judge only the presence of such markers and not whether the topic is important.
proposals.rationale: Trend-compatible vocabulary can make an abstract easier to recognize within a current research community without indicating quality. Examples include the LLM- and agent-centered framing of R17 and R50.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission time and field fashion

proposals.name: Stock abstract cadence
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract follows a conventional problem-gap-method-evaluation-release sequence with formulaic transitions; judge only the extent of this template and not whether the resulting exposition is good.
proposals.rationale: Familiar templates can make entries easier to process, while experienced authors may also communicate real ideas more clearly. Examples include R04 and R41.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the abstract format

proposals.name: Mechanistic Explanation over Empirical Success
proposals.instruction: 0 = purely empirical results, heuristic fixes, or benchmark performance without explaining the underlying causes. 10 = the abstract centers on deriving deep mechanistic explanations, dynamics, or mathematical proofs for *why* a phenomenon occurs.
proposals.rationale: R08, R15, R57, and R58 focus heavily on explaining the underlying mechanics of their respective phenomena, which the dense model likely perceives as high-quality research, whereas R06, R12, and R54 rely on engineering fixes without deep mechanistic insight.

proposals.name: Fundamental Inductive Bias from First Principles
proposals.instruction: 0 = approach relies on ad-hoc engineering combinations, heuristic losses, or hyperparameter tuning. 10 = introduces a new architectural component, constraint, or inductive bias derived purely from first principles, geometry, or physical constraints.
proposals.rationale: R27, R34, R45, and R49 introduce highly principled structural biases derived from theory, explaining the dense model's high scores compared to R13, R42, and R54, which combine existing modules heuristically.

proposals.name: Formal Discovery of Universal Laws or Limits
proposals.instruction: 0 = the paper makes incremental, task-specific empirical gains. 10 = mathematically establishes fundamental limits, scaling laws, or universal functional forms (e.g., generalization bounds, rate-distortion limits).
proposals.rationale: R10, R14, R44, and R60 establish universal laws and bounds that the dense model values highly, in stark contrast to R28 and R46, which focus on narrow empirical setups.

proposals.name: Conceptual Simplification via Deconstruction
proposals.instruction: 0 = blindly adds complexity, patches known issues, or stacks modules. 10 = systematically deconstructs a complex model to mathematically isolate the minimal essential components required for success.
proposals.rationale: R25 and R58 deconstruct complex paradigms (diffusion models, classifiers) to find the minimal essential components, a profound research quality missed by the scorecard but caught by the dense model, unlike the patching approaches in R06 and R54.

proposals.name: Mathematical Formulation of Informal Concepts
proposals.instruction: 0 = uses standard, pre-existing definitions or leaves key concepts vague and unformalized. 10 = rigorously formalizes a previously vague or informal intuition into a precise mathematical framework.
proposals.rationale: R08, R09, and R29 formalize abstract ideas into precise mathematical frameworks, a depth likely perceived by the dense model but missed by the scorecard, whereas R17 and R18 leave concepts more empirically defined.

proposals.name: Principled Problem Reformulation
proposals.instruction: 0 = applies standard methods to an existing problem formulation without changing the core mathematical objective. 10 = fundamentally reframes an existing problem in a completely new mathematical light.
proposals.rationale: R01, R36, R40, and R47 reformulate their respective problems fundamentally (e.g., as a transport problem), explaining the dense model's preference over R41 and R55, which merely tweak existing setups.

proposals.name: Conceptual Depth over Trendy Application
proposals.instruction: 0 = value proposition leans entirely on trendy surface-level keywords (e.g., LLM agents, benchmarks) without core algorithmic advances. 10 = deeply explores core ML mechanisms, offering profound insights independent of application hype.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors R35, R47, and R58 for deep core ML theory, while rejecting R11, R16, R24, and R28, which rely heavily on LLM and benchmark hype without fundamental theoretical contributions.

proposals.name: Theory-Driven Efficiency Gains
proposals.instruction: 0 = efficiency improvements result from system-level engineering, hardware tuning, or quantization tricks. 10 = massive efficiency gains are a direct mathematical consequence of a novel theoretical insight.
proposals.rationale: R02, R27, and R36 achieve massive efficiency through mathematical insight, explaining the dense model's high scores, whereas R05 and R56 achieve efficiency via system-level scaling and engineering.

proposals.name: Intrinsic Property Analysis
proposals.instruction: 0 = evaluation and goals are entirely focused on extrinsic performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, success rate). 10 = central contribution is proving or analyzing intrinsic structural, geometric, or topological properties of the model.
proposals.rationale: R15, R25, R31, and R47 analyze intrinsic geometric properties of representations and weights, which the dense model recognizes as high quality, while R23, R37, and R54 focus purely on extrinsic attack/detection success rates.

proposals.name: Generalizable Theoretical Guarantees
proposals.instruction: 0 = theoretical claims are highly task-specific or rely on narrow, qualified assumptions. 10 = provides theorems, bounds, or mathematical proofs that apply broadly across multiple architectures or dimensions.
proposals.rationale: R14, R35, and R44 offer broad theoretical guarantees across multiple architectures, a key differentiator for the dense model over R12 and R50, whose theoretical claims are narrower.

proposals.name: Predictive Framework Formulation
proposals.instruction: 0 = theory is only used post-hoc to justify empirical observations. 10 = the proposed theoretical framework is actively used to predict unseen behaviors, future scaling limits, or out-of-sample errors.
proposals.rationale: R10, R44, and R60 use their frameworks to make novel predictions about model scale and fundamental limits, a highly valued property missed by the scorecard, unlike R04 and R42 which fit theory to existing data.

proposals.name: Algorithmic Novelty Native to ML
proposals.instruction: 0 = applies existing algorithms imported from other domains or combines known heuristic losses. 10 = proposes a fundamentally new optimization algorithm or geometric mapping native to machine learning.
proposals.rationale: R30, R45, and R47 derive novel algorithms natively for ML representations, which the dense model scores highly, whereas R13 and R39 import metrics and algorithms from external fields like computational geometry.

proposals.name: Focus on Structural Model Modifications
proposals.instruction: 0 = modifies data pipelines, loss weights, or training hyperparameters while keeping the architecture intact. 10 = alters the core mathematical structure of the model, introducing new attention mechanisms or fundamental architectural shifts.
proposals.rationale: R25, R27, R32, and R34 introduce structural architectural changes that the dense model values, whereas R12, R50, and R55 restrict their modifications to data and loss functions.

proposals.name: Rigorous Bounds vs Heuristic Trade-offs
proposals.instruction: 0 = discovers an empirical, ad-hoc trade-off between two conflicting metrics. 10 = mathematically establishes rigorous bounds, optimal trade-offs, or fundamental optimality conditions.
proposals.rationale: R29, R40, and R60 establish optimal mathematical bounds, explaining the dense model's preference, while R41 and R42 merely describe an empirical trade-off between conflicting metrics.

proposals.name: Task-Agnostic Foundational Contribution
proposals.instruction: 0 = proposes a solution heavily overfitted to a highly specific niche application. 10 = proposes a foundational primitive (e.g., a new layer, theorem, or universal bound) that is task-agnostic and broadly applicable.
proposals.rationale: R26, R30, R34, and R58 provide foundational primitives applicable across many domains, which the scorecard undervalues compared to the dense model, while R03, R21, and R53 are hyper-specific to niche applications.

proposals.name: Abstract Word Count
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract is exceptionally long or wordy, from 0 (very short/concise) to 10 (excessively long/verbose). Do not judge the quality of the writing, only the sheer volume of text.
proposals.rationale: Text length often biases automated evaluation models independent of the core insight. The dense model might favor highly concise abstracts (e.g., R34 is very brief), while the scorecard model might score longer, more detailed abstracts higher simply because they contain more checkable words (e.g., R60 is exceptionally long).
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Promotional Intensifiers
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract uses heavily promotional or subjective intensifiers (e.g., 'remarkably', 'strikingly', 'immensely', 'breakthrough'), from 0 (none) to 10 (excessive). Do not judge if the claims are true, only count the promotional language.
proposals.rationale: Professional editing or marketing practices often inject these intensifiers to artificially boost a paper's reception, leaving a clear textual fingerprint. R05 uses phrases like 'immensely effective' and 'highly popular', while R07 uses 'Remarkably'. R60 uses 'breakthrough performance'. These can inflate a scorecard without correlating to actual research quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: professional editing or marketing assistance

proposals.name: Large-Scale Compute Flexing
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract highlights access to massive computational resources or unprecedented scale (e.g., GPUs, TPU pods, billions of parameters) as a primary feature, from 0 (none) to 10 (heavy emphasis).
proposals.rationale: Access to upstream institutional funding and large-scale compute allows authors to brute-force benchmarks. The textual fingerprint is explicit boasting about hardware or model size. R10 highlights using the 'memory limit of a TPUv3 Pod', and R60 emphasizes '175 billion parameters' and 'GPU hours'. This reflects resources, not necessarily algorithmic quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional funding and compute resources

proposals.name: Math Notation Density
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract contains dense mathematical notation, LaTeX formatting, variables, and formal definitions, from 0 (none) to 10 (very dense). Do not judge the correctness of the math, only its visible presence.
proposals.rationale: Theoretical sub-fields have different norms that leave a heavy fingerprint of inline math. R40 uses matrix notation ($A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$), and R59 discusses RKHS and Gaussian universality. A scorecard model might blindly award points for this apparent rigor, while a dense text model might penalize the low readability.
proposals.upstream_parent: sub-field norms (theoretical ML)

proposals.name: Trend-Chasing Hyper-recency
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract reads like a late-arriving riff on a highly current, already-saturated trend (e.g., LLMs, GPT, NeRF), rather than an original foundational problem. 0 for foundational, 10 for heavily derivative trending topic.
proposals.rationale: Items submitted late in the conference cycle often latch onto the latest buzzwords to stay relevant. R20 leverages 'dynamic-NeRF' for an adversarial attack, and R60 focuses squarely on compressing 'Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT or OPT)'. This indicates authors reacting to the current hype cycle rather than pursuing deeper, timeless questions.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / submission timing

proposals.name: Named Benchmark Reliance
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract relies heavily on listing established dataset names and standard benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet, GLUE, COCO) as a structural crutch, from 0 (none) to 10 (excessive namedropping).
proposals.rationale: The upstream community's focus on leaderboards creates an incentive to name-drop benchmarks. R37 explicitly lists 'COCO2017', and R40 lists the 'GLUE benchmark'. An author can achieve high benchmark performance through incremental tuning, which leaves a fingerprint of heavy benchmark reliance that may trick a scorecard model.
proposals.upstream_parent: community focus on leaderboards

proposals.name: Method Acronym Branding
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract invents and heavily promotes a specific, capitalized acronym for its method or model (e.g., LAMB, FLAG), from 0 (none) to 10 (method is only referred to by a heavily branded acronym).
proposals.rationale: Authors increasingly practice 'branding' their methods to increase memorability, which is a marketing tactic rather than a research contribution. R10 introduces 'LAMB', R19 introduces 'FLAG', and R17 introduces 'NeRN'. This typographical habit can bias models that look for proper nouns.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format / marketing

proposals.name: Boilerplate Structural Formula
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract follows a rigid, boilerplate template (e.g., 'In this paper, we propose...', 'Extensive experiments show...'), from 0 (fluid narrative) to 10 (strict, copy-pasted formulaic structure).
proposals.rationale: Less experienced authors often copy structural templates, leaving rigid, predictable transitions. R36, R37, and R39 all rely heavily on the exact same boilerplate phrasing ('In this paper, we suggest/propose...'). This structural rigidity is a fingerprint of inexperience in academic writing.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Defensive Consensus Challenging
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract uses explicit phrasing to claim it is challenging a consensus, debunking an open secret, or resolving a widespread misconception, from 0 to 10. Do not judge if the consensus is real.
proposals.rationale: Authors sometimes manufacture a 'strawman' consensus to elevate their work's perceived importance. R35 explicitly states 'This consensus, however, is challenged in this paper', and R45 begins by naming an 'open secret in contemporary machine learning'. This is a rhetorical framing tactic that can artificially inflate relevance.
proposals.upstream_parent: rhetorical strategy / framing

proposals.name: Code Link Inclusion
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract explicitly includes a URL to a GitHub repository or project page, from 0 (no link) to 10 (link prominently featured).
proposals.rationale: The inclusion of a URL is a textual fingerprint of modern open-source practices and project management. R04, R07, R20, and R48 all include explicit links. A scorecard model might award points simply for the presence of a link, treating it as a proxy for reproducibility, even though the text itself cannot verify the code's quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: process dynamics on the receiving side / open-source practices

proposals.name: Formal Mathematical Derivation Density
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly claims a rigorous mathematical derivation, proof, or theoretical bound that directly motivates the method (e.g., using terms like 'provable', 'theorem', 'derivation', 'bounds'). Score 0 if the method is entirely heuristic or empirical with no formal mathematical foundation.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors deep theoretical grounding, as seen in theoretical works on offline RL (R24) and linear estimation (R50), which a standard scorecard might miss by only checking for empirical performance keywords.

proposals.name: Mechanistic Deconstruction as Discovery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper systematically strips down or deconstructs a complex system to isolate the essential mechanisms causing an effect (e.g., identifying that 'only a few components are critical'). Score 0 if the system is treated as a monolithic black box.
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly values scientific inquiry into why models work, rewarding papers that carefully isolate fundamental components (R30, R43) over mere engineering.

proposals.name: Benchmark-Centric Framing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the primary contribution is the introduction of a new dataset, benchmark, or evaluation suite, with methods playing a secondary role. Score 0 if it is a pure algorithmic or theoretical contribution with no new datasets.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard may over-credit abstracts heavily featuring a new 'Bench' or dataset (R14, R56), while the dense model perceives this as lacking fundamental algorithmic or theoretical research quality.

proposals.name: Novel Core Architectural Primitive
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract introduces a completely new mathematical operation or topological structure at the core of a neural network (e.g., higher-dimensional attention, novel tensor products). Score 0 if it uses standard architectures with only external modules or hyperparameter tweaks.
proposals.rationale: The dense model strongly credits structural innovations to a network's core mathematical operations (R01, R33), which a scorecard might underweight compared to standard task performance.

proposals.name: Explicit Formalization of Inductive Bias
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly grounds its model in an assumed mathematical, physical, or logical structure (e.g., PDEs, simplex ETFs, molecular motifs). Score 0 if the architecture has no explicit mapping to an underlying mathematical/physical structure.
proposals.rationale: The dense model recognizes when a model accurately reflects the geometry or physics of the problem (R02, R32), a subtle property scorecards miss by looking at general performance.

proposals.name: Overclaiming Impact from Narrow Tuning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract frames an engineering, scaling, or hyperparameter optimization (e.g., training speedup, quantization) as a fundamental breakthrough. Score 0 if claims are modest and strictly limited to the specific engineering gains.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard may over-credit large performance numbers or system speedups (R44, R59), which the dense model views as incremental engineering rather than fundamental research.

proposals.name: Counter-Intuitive Scientific Finding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract highlights a surprising or paradoxical phenomenon that challenges conventional wisdom (e.g., 'removing clean images boosts robustness'). Score 0 if the results are exactly what one would expect from standard methods.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards the identification of deep paradoxes or surprising insights (R55, R33), indicating high scientific value that rigid scorecards fail to capture.

proposals.name: Trend-Surfing via Model Stitching
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the main contribution is mechanically applying a current buzzword (e.g., LLMs, NeRF, Hyperbolic spaces) to an unrelated domain without fundamental integration. Score 0 if concepts are deeply, principled integrated or no trendy concepts are used.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard over-credits abstracts that stitch together trendy models (R10, R16), whereas the dense model discounts this superficiality, preferring fundamental methods.

proposals.name: Information-Theoretic Grounding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the problem is formulated using foundational concepts from information theory, probability, or statistics (e.g., rate-distortion, KL divergence, Bayes-optimal policies). Score 0 if ad-hoc losses or heuristic rules are used.
proposals.rationale: The dense model heavily weights papers rooted in fundamental limits or information theory (R27, R31), which requires deep understanding beyond simple scorecard keyword matching.

proposals.name: Definition of a New Fundamental Limit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper establishes a new theoretical ceiling, floor, or bound for a general class of problems (e.g., generalization bounds across scales, cost of overfitting). Score 0 if it focuses only on heuristic performance improvements.
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly values characterizing the theoretical limits of learning (R07, R46), a conceptual leap missed by scorecards looking for empirical state-of-the-art results.

proposals.name: Formal Analysis of Optimization Dynamics
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract provides rigorous mathematical analysis of optimization dynamics, convergence rates, or loss landscape geometry. Score 0 if training is treated as a black box with no analysis of dynamics.
proposals.rationale: The dense model credits papers that mathematically explain the behavior of training algorithms (R53, R43), contrasting with scorecards that may just reward the final empirical outcome.

proposals.name: Surface-Level Safety Framing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract relies heavily on 'safety', 'adversarial', or 'attack' buzzwords to frame a heuristic method without deep theoretical formulation. Score 0 if it avoids these buzzwords or provides rigorous mathematical treatment of robustness.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard over-credits safety/adversarial framing (R10, R21), while the dense model looks for actual rigorous robustness theory.

proposals.name: Structural Innovation with Theoretical Guarantee
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract proposes a completely new architectural structure AND provides a mathematical theorem or bound proving its specific properties. Score 0 if it proposes a structure with only empirical justification, or a theorem without a new structure.
proposals.rationale: The dense model assigns the highest value when structural novelty and theoretical proof are combined (R20, R47), a dual requirement often flattened by rigid scorecards.

proposals.name: Explicit Formalization of Uncertainty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core method explicitly models, bounds, or reasons about epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty. Score 0 if the model produces point estimates with no formal handling of uncertainty.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors principled handling of the unknown (R24, R22), a subtle methodological strength that a scorecard might miss if it only checks for task metrics.

proposals.name: Surplus Algorithmic Complexity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract describes a method that simply stacks multiple known complex modules (e.g., ensembles, multiple transformers) without a unifying mathematical simplification. Score 0 if the method introduces a simple, elegant rule that replaces complex heuristics.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard may over-credit complex systems that combine multiple modules for marginal gains (R19, R48), which the dense model discounts in favor of elegant simplifications.

proposals.name: Explicit contribution-claim boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract uses template phrases that explicitly announce contributions (e.g., “we propose”, “we introduce”, “we present”, “we address”, “to the best of our knowledge”, “for the first time”). Score 0 for none, 10 for pervasive use. Do not judge whether this is good or bad; score only how much is present.
proposals.rationale: A scorecard keyed to explicit criteria may reward visible contribution claims, while a dense reader may discount them. The slice shows this split: R03 foregrounds “we propose a 3D promptable segmentation model” and R05 foregrounds “we propose a novel data-driven approach”, both typical boilerplate announcements.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's familiarity with conference writing templates

proposals.name: Branded system or acronym naming
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract coins or foregrounds a catchy system name or acronym (e.g., “ImpScore”, “Point-SAM”, “VariBAD”, “ProtoSnap”). Score 0 for no coined name, 10 for multiple emphasized branded names. Do not judge whether naming is effective; score only how much branding is present.
proposals.rationale: Catchy names can make an entry seem more established than it is. R03 (Point-SAM) and R30 (VariBAD) both push a branded name into the title and abstract, a surface signal a dense model may overweight while a scorecard ignores it.
proposals.upstream_parent: marketing/branding strategy

proposals.name: Hard performance numbers in abstract
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract includes specific quantitative performance figures, records, or large dataset/model sizes (e.g., “30% to 73%”, “76 minutes”, “18K questions”, “175 billion parameters”). Score 0 for none, 10 for many. Do not judge whether the numbers are impressive; score only how many are present.
proposals.rationale: Concrete numbers satisfy explicit evaluation criteria but can also bait a dense reader. R04 quotes a jump “from 30% to 73%” and R53 cites “175 billion parameters” in four GPU hours, both numeric anchors that are predictive yet not inherently quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's reporting practice and data availability

proposals.name: Formal notation density
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract uses dense mathematical notation, formal definitions, or symbolic variables (e.g., “A ∈ ℝ^{n×d}”, “ε_adv”, SVD). Score 0 for plain prose, 10 for heavily symbolic text. Do not judge whether the notation is correct or useful; score only how much appears.
proposals.rationale: Symbolic density can make an entry look technically deep regardless of substance. R23 embeds matrix-algebra notation directly in the abstract and R49 uses adversarial-budget symbols, a register that may sway a dense model but not a checklist-based one.
proposals.upstream_parent: subfield epistemic norms (theory vs applied)

proposals.name: Trend-buzzword density
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract foregrounds currently fashionable keywords (e.g., “large language model”, “agent”, “diffusion”, “transformer”, “benchmark”, “foundation model”). Score 0 for none, 10 for pervasive use. Do not judge whether the topic is important; score only how many buzzwords appear.
proposals.rationale: Trendy vocabulary may attract attention irrespective of rigor. R05 is saturated with “LLM agents” and “proactive” framing, while R22 leads with “knowledge fusion of large language models”, both heavy on fashionable terms a dense reader may overvalue.
proposals.upstream_parent: topic fashion / bandwagon

proposals.name: Large-resource / compute scale mentions
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract signals access to large-scale computational resources, massive datasets, or industrial-scale infrastructure (e.g., “TPUv3 Pod”, “850K instruction pairs”, “175 billion parameters”). Score 0 for none, 10 for heavy emphasis. Do not judge whether large scale is desirable; score only how much is mentioned.
proposals.rationale: Compute scale enables big experiments but is a resource signal rather than a quality of the idea. R14 stresses “TPUv3 Pod” and 76-minute BERT training, and R53 emphasizes a 175B-parameter model run on a single GPU, both of which may impress a dense model more than a scorecard.
proposals.upstream_parent: access to compute / institutional resources

proposals.name: Authoritative framing and named baselines
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract uses confident, authoritative language (e.g., “first rigorous study”, “best-known”, “state-of-the-art”) and name-drops many high-profile systems as baselines. Score 0 for tentative or generic framing, 10 for highly authoritative, name-saturated prose. Do not judge whether the confidence is warranted; score only how much authoritative framing appears.
proposals.rationale: Senior authors often write with an authoritative register that a dense model may read as quality. R20 claims “best-known theoretical guarantees” and R38 calls its study “the first rigorous” of its kind, both signals of standing rather than inherent merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: author reputation / seniority in the field

proposals.name: Surface polish and typographic perfection
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract is free of typos, grammatical errors, and formatting quirks, exhibiting a uniformly professional copyedited style. Score 0 for many errors, 10 for flawless polish. Do not judge whether polish makes the paper better; score only how clean the text is.
proposals.rationale: A polished surface can make an entry read as higher quality than its substance warrants. R04 and R42 are both typographically immaculate and smoothly phrased, the kind of finish that may bias a dense reader while adding nothing to the research content.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing assistance / proofreading

proposals.name: Promotional / PR markers
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract includes promotional language, shortened URLs, project-page references, or social-media-ready handles beyond a simple code link. Score 0 for none, 10 for many promotional markers. Do not judge whether promotion is useful; score only how much is present.
proposals.rationale: PR effort can inflate perceived importance. R11 points to a Google Sites project page and R37 uses a bit.ly short link, both hallmarks of active promotion that a dense model may mistake for community traction.
proposals.upstream_parent: marketing/PR effort

proposals.name: Obvious-template vs late-riff register
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract reads as a direct, obvious application of a well-known framework to a new domain (e.g., “X works in 2D; we extend it to 3D”) versus a late-arriving, highly specialized riff that assumes many prior takes are already known. Score 0 for a highly specialized late-riff style, 10 for an obvious first-pass template style. Do not judge which style is better; score only the extent to which it reads as an obvious first-pass take.
proposals.rationale: Early entries in a crowded contest often read as obvious readings of the prompt, while late entries assume the obvious takes are taken. R03 reads as a direct “SAM → 3D points” template and R11 reads as an on-trend “LLM agent + open world” take, both fingerprints of timing and position rather than research quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / submission timing
